source_citation: Le Morte d'Arthur (Malory, 1485) Book IV: Galatine is Gawain's sword, given by the Lady of the Lake; described as so bright it blinds opponents — holy-radiance register; also appears in Lancelot do Lac (13th C Vulgate Cycle)

Alliterative Morte Arthure (14th C): Clarent is Arthur's ceremonial sword of peace (not war), stolen by Mordred and used to slay Arthur — treachery and shadow coding; Le Morte d'Arthur (Malory) corroborates the Mordred-theft narrative

Culhwch and Olwen (Mabinogion, 11th-12th C compilation): Carnwennan (Little White-Hilt) is one of Arthur's Thirteen Treasures of Britain; the knife could shrink into shadow to kill Orddu the witch — canonical shadow-cloaking attribute; Trioedd Ynys Prydein (Welsh Triads) lists it among Arthur's treasures

Chanson de Roland (11th-12th C): Almace is the sword of Archbishop Turpin, one of Charlemagne's twelve peers; Turpin wields it at Roncevaux as a clerical-warrior — consecrated register via churchman-bearer; Turpin's death scene in the Roland tradition is one of the most cited clerical-weapon passages in Old French epic

Völsunga saga ch. 14-16: Gram is reforged by Regin for Sigurd; Sigurd uses Gram to slay Fafnir the dragon; Poetic Edda (Fáfnismál, Reginsmál): Gram is the sharpest of swords — fire association through dragon-slaying + the sword's original shattering and reforging in the fire of the smithy; also named in Grímnismál

cultural_tradition: European grimoire / folk-magic (English + French tradition; Main de Gloire)
form: focus (severed hand as lantern-caster implement; sleep-inducing magical relic)
source_citation: Petit Albert (French grimoire, 18th C compilation of older folk-tradition; Main de Gloire recipe); Yorkshire Museum specimen (physical artifact); Grose's Provincial Glossary (1787, documents English tradition tracing to medieval burglary-magic); Middleton's Witch (1613) pre-dates the Petit Albert print — attests to older English theatrical circulation of the concept

cultural_tradition: Latin Christian / Crusader relic tradition (Holy Lance)
form: spear (relic-lance; sacred implement of the Passion)
source_citation: Gospel of John 19:34 (soldier pierces Jesus's side — source-event); Chronicle of the First Crusade (Raymond d'Agiles, 1098): Peter Bartholomew's vision locates the lance at Antioch; the Antioch relic authenticated by Urban II; Vienna Hofburg Spear (medieval artifact claiming to be the Holy Lance); Longinus legend in Legenda Aurea (Jacobus de Voragine, 13th C)

Poetic Edda (Eddic verse): Hófuð (Man's-Head, also glossed as Head-ransom) is the name of Heimdall's sword per kenning-traditions; Heimdall is the Aesir watchman who guards Bifrost against giants — his sword and the Gjallarhorn are his canonical implements; Snorri Sturluson corroborates Heimdall as armed guardian in Gylfaginning

form: sword (Saracen enchanted sword; fire-register via jewel-name)
source_citation: Chanson d'Aspremont (12th C Old French epic): Précieuse (Precious One) is the named sword of the Saracen king Agolant; Roland takes it as a trophy — cross-cultural trophy-capture narrative; the Chanson d'Aspremont is the named source per medieval epic scholarship (Meredith-Jones 1936 edition; Mandach 1961)
